title: Measuring the Marginal Value of Sandboxed Emulation for Validator‑Checked LLM‑Generated NetOps Artifacts
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study that measured the marginal detection benefit of adding sandboxed emulation to a deterministic validator for LLM-generated intent→configuration artifacts. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics using the declared model "gpt-5-mini" (provider recorded as openai_responses) we evaluated Npairs = 720 confirmatory tasks drawn from a deterministic synthetic task generator. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) flagged 719/720 = 0.9986111111111111; the guarded pipeline (validator + sandboxed emulation) flagged 720/720 = 1.0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.001388888888888884; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.004166666666666667]. These results are far below our preregistered minimum effect-of-interest (0.20). We report the preregistered design, exact artifact-grounded outcomes, provider-call/run-accounting reconciliation, interpretation for the negligible marginal guarded benefit in this regime, and concise reproducibility pointers into the archived execution bundle.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configuration and NetOps workflows. Operational deployment requires generated artifacts to satisfy syntactic correctness, workflow ordering, and higher-order safety/policy constraints. A common mitigation architecture is generate→validate→(repair)→execute, sometimes augmented by sandboxed emulation to reveal runtime-only failures that static validators may miss. Prior surveys and system reports document this workflow-centred approach and motivate careful evaluation of each stage [1]–[3].

Research question and contributions. Our preregistered research question was: for synthetic intent→configuration tasks under shared_initial_candidate semantics, what is the paired detection‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) between (A) a deterministic validator-only pipeline and (B) the same deterministic validator followed by automated sandboxed emulation? We contribute: (1) a faithful preregistered paired confirmatory design and execution; (2) an artifact-grounded paired analysis on Npairs = 720 with full run accounting; (3) a concise, evidence-based interpretation of a near-zero marginal effect in this constrained regime; (4) reproducibility pointers and prescriptive boundary conditions where guarded stages are most likely to matter.
sections.related_work:
Workflow-centred mitigations and verification tools. Recent surveys and architecture papers synthesize the practical trend of pairing LLM generation with deterministic validators, emulators, and repair loops to raise operational assurance for NetOps artifacts [1], and they summarize prototype systems that combine generation, rule-based checking, and executable validation [2]. Tool-focused case studies document the evolution of static verifiers (expanded rule-sets, topology-aware checks) and identify gaps for runtime-dependent behaviors and stateful sequences; this motivates layering emulation after static validation to exercise temporal behaviors and interactions that static checks may not capture [2], [3].

Empirical evidence and evaluation gaps. Prototype studies report heterogeneous gains from guarded pipelines: in some regimes a strong static verifier catches most dangerous errors, in others emulation uncovers subtle runtime failures. The literature therefore emphasizes workload- and validator‑sensitivity and calls for controlled, workflow-centred measurements of guarded-stage marginal value—precisely the narrow question our paired shared_initial_candidate design isolates [1]–[3].
sections.methodology:
Overview and preregistration. We preregistered a paired-binary confirmatory protocol (study_id f2c3d8b1-7a6e-4a9a-b2c3-5f8e1d2b6c7e). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline aggregated across confirmatory samples; a minimum effect-of-interest = 0.20 was used for power planning. The preregistration fixed inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness handling (deterministic reseed up to two times for parser failures), multiplicity handling for exploratory secondary tests, and deterministic contamination controls.

Task bank, vendors and topology templates. Confirmatory items were generated deterministically from the intent_configuration_repair_v1 family. The bank covers three abstracted vendor‑CLI families and three topology templates (leaf–spine, 3-node service chain, triangle). Each task manifest contains the initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit natural-language intent, a required_command_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and workflow policies (e.g., make-before-break). Inclusion required vendor-parser acceptance after at most two deterministic reseeds; in the confirmatory run there were zero irrecoverable parser exclusions and complete_pair_count = 720.

Model and shared_initial_candidate enforcement. The declared/requested model was recorded as "gpt-5-mini" (provider: openai_responses) and archived in the model-configuration artifact. For each task we obtained exactly one sampled initial candidate (a single provider call) and presented that identical candidate to both downstream conditions (baseline and guarded). This shared_initial_candidate semantics isolates downstream guarded-stage effects (emulation observations or permitted repairs) from generation variability.

Baseline validator. The baseline validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) is deterministic and rule-based. Its checks include vendor-CLI syntactic parsing; per-command canonicalization; sequence-order checks against required_command_sequence; atomicity and workflow constraints (make-before-break, all_down_before_any_field_change); protected-interface invariants; group-level activity constraints; and final-state conformance tests. The validator emits a binary detection flag and a validator_trace object documenting parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and any violation codes.

Guarded pipeline and emulation harness. The guarded pipeline runs the baseline validator and then executes the same candidate in a sandboxed-emulation harness instantiated from the task’s topology template. The emulation harness records runtime observations (interface transitions, concurrent-interface states, MTU/VLAN application effects, and observable reachability) and maps them to runtime-observation rules that can trigger a guarded detection when they reveal policy or safety violations not encoded as static validator rules. The emulation mapping used conservative detection rules so that emulation-triggered detections indicate observable runtime policy breaches.

Repair policy and run accounting. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one repair-stage model invocation per task and only after guarded observations were available. Provider-call auditing recorded model_calls_used = 721 with stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 720 and repair = 1. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics were enforced, any discordant pair (guarded-only detection) must be attributable to either an emulation-observed runtime violation or to the single recorded repair invocation; per-episode artifacts record these links.

Provider-call audit fields and reconciliation (clarification requested by reviewers). The execution manifest's provider-call audit summarizes hosted-model call events by stage and by whether a call was shared across conditions or unique to a condition. Key audit fields:
- stage_counts: per-stage counts (e.g., shared_initial_generation = 720, repair = 1) indicate how many provider calls were executed in each pipeline stage across the run.
- condition_counts: counts labeled "shared" denote calls executed during the shared_initial_generation stage whose outputs were presented to both paired conditions; counts labeled "guarded" denote calls executed only by the guarded pipeline (for example, repair calls). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics we expect asymmetry: a single shared initial generation call per pair yields 720 shared calls, while repair calls occur only when the guarded path invokes them (here only once), producing condition_counts that may show "shared":720 and "guarded":1. The overall provider_call audit reconciles to model_calls_used = sum(stage_counts) = 721. Deterministic_reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 720, completed_episode_count = 1440, and zero failed episodes; these reconciliations and per-episode links are archived for independent verification.
sections.results:
Primary confirmatory counts and inferential outputs (artifact-grounded). The paired contingency counts are n11 = 719 (detected by both), n10 = 1 (guarded-only), n01 = 0 (baseline-only), n00 = 0 (neither). Marginal detection rates: baseline = 719/720 = 0.9986111111111111; guarded = 720/720 = 1.0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.001388888888888884. Exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.004166666666666667]. All reported numeric values are verbatim from the archived analysis artifacts.

Discordant-pair attribution and repair accounting. Provider-call auditing and deterministic reconciliation identify a single repair-stage invocation and the single n10 discordant count. Because the same initial candidate was supplied to both conditions, the unique guarded-only detection corresponds to the sole repair-stage invocation recorded (i.e., the audited repair call produced the downstream guarded detection) or to an emulation observation traceable in the archived per-episode artifacts; the execution bundle contains the exact per-episode record that links pair_id → validator_trace → repair_provider_trace so an auditor can inspect whether the guarded-only flag resulted from the documented repair call or from an emulation-only observation.

Representative per-episode diagnostics. Representative scoring traces (validator_trace) include normalized_configuration, validation_before/after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation_count. In the confirmatory set the vast majority of shared_initial candidates complied with validator rules (violation_count = 0) and sandboxed emulation corroborated the static checks in these curated cases; this pattern is consistent with the observed near-ceiling baseline success rate.
sections.discussion:
Why the guarded-stage aggregate benefit was negligible. Three artifact-grounded factors explain the near-zero marginal effect in this experimental regime.

1) Validator ceiling effect and task-rule alignment. The deterministic validator explicitly encodes the workflow and safety constraints present in the curated task payloads (patterns such as shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). Representative validator_trace fields show parsed_command_count and required_command_count consistent with complete static coverage in most cases, producing a baseline success rate of 719/720.

2) Curated inclusion and reduced adversarial exposure. Confirmatory items required parser acceptance and were generated by a deterministic generator. This inclusion policy concentrates the task bank where a strong static validator achieves high coverage and underrepresents the adversarial and noisy inputs where emulation typically reveals additional runtime issues.

3) Shared_initial_candidate semantics and limited repair activity. Reusing the exact sampled initial candidate for both conditions removes generation variability as a source of discordance; the single discordant episode therefore maps to the single recorded repair-stage call (or to an emulation observation recorded in that episode). Provider-call accounting (model_calls_used = 721; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 720, repair = 1) and deterministic_reconciliation provide an auditable mapping from the reported aggregate counts to the unique discordant episode.

Operational implications. For environments that enforce strong parser-based inclusion and maintain a high-coverage static validator tuned to expected intent patterns, an automated sandboxed-emulation stage may produce little incremental detection benefit at scale. This is a conditional finding: it does not imply emulation is unnecessary. Guarded stages remain valuable for (a) noisy natural-language intents, (b) adversarial or fuzzed inputs that exercise validator gaps, (c) broader multi‑vendor CLI diversity, and (d) complex long‑lived state transitions that are hard to codify as static rules. Practically, operators should consider investing in richer static validators for high-throughput intent→config pipelines and applying guarded sandboxing selectively for high‑risk changes. The archived execution artifacts provide concrete seed cases to guide adversarial test‑case design and targeted validator improvement.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a deterministic validator to the same validator augmented by sandboxed emulation on a curated synthetic intent→configuration task bank. Over 720 paired tasks the guarded pipeline produced a negligible aggregate detection gain (0.001388888888888884) with exact McNemar p = 1.0 and 95% bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.004166666666666667]. Run accounting shows a single repair-stage invocation corresponding to the unique guarded-only detection; archived per-episode traces permit independent verification. We interpret the near-zero aggregate effect as arising from validator ceiling effects and the curated, parser-validated task design. Extensions prioritizing adversarial task generation, greater vendor diversity, and higher-fidelity emulation are required to identify regimes where guarded stages offer substantive operational value.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and deterministic task generator produce limited ecological diversity and create a validator-ceiling effect; results may not generalize to noisier, adversarial, or production distributions.
Single declared/requested model family (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) limit generalizability across models and validator families.

Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation reused across paired conditions) isolate guarded-stage contributions but remove potential generation-based remediation benefits that an independent guarded-generation policy could provide.

Sandboxed-emulation fidelity relative to vendor/OS production behaviors and long-lived stateful interactions is limited by the emulation harness used; higher-fidelity emulators could change outcomes in other regimes.

Study power planning targeted a minimum detectable paired difference of 0.20; the observed aggregate effect (~0.0014) lies far below that design sensitivity and should be interpreted as a narrowly scoped near-zero finding for this experimental regime rather than a general negative result for all NetOps workflows.

Provider-side nondeterminism and hidden caching remain residual uncertainties despite deterministic reconciliation procedures; these are documented in the archived execution manifest and reconciliation artifacts.
